 6. The trial court, on considering the provisions of Presidents Order No. 26 of 1972 held that the Sonali Bank was the successor-in-interest of the National Bank of Pakistan and therefore had, the right of recovery of the debt owing to that Bank. After considering the evidence and materials on record in further held that the suit was not barred by limitation and also not bad for non-joinder of the Government and the Jute Corporation. 

 17. The main trend of the Counsel's argument seemed to veer round the Government's taking over the jute business of the appellant company along with its jute stocks which were offered as security for the repayment of the loan. Mr. Ahmed quite vehemently asserted that when the Government of the country took over the entire Ispahani Group of Industries including the properties hypothecated to the predecessor of the Sonali Bank, respondent No. I, against which the appellant company had no remedy, respondent No. 1 should have, in all fairness, proceeded against the Government. Liability to repay the loan is inseparable from the assets against which the loan was obtained. Since the assets against which the loans were advanced passing over to the Government, the liability to repay which attached to it also passed to the Government. The appellant company must be considered to have been released of its obligation to repay. Appellant's Counsel, while referring to the Government which appointed an Administrator and the subsequent transfer of the company's assets and liabilities to the Jute Corporation and Jute Marketing Corporation successively, submitted that the suit was not maintainable in the absence of either the Government or the Jute Marketing Corporation who as it appears, were not impleaded in the suit by the respondent bank. According to him, therefore, the suit was bad for non-joinder of necessary parties and liable to be dismissed. 

 33. For the first time this grievance is being raised before this Court. Had it been so real a grievance for which it now claims to be absolved of its liability to the Bank the company had ample opportunities to do so either by taking the objection in the written statement or before the framing of issues or even during the trial. The Counsel pointed out that the company took twenty-one adjournments for filing the written statement for twenty-one times and finally filed it after the Court fixed the case for exparte hearing on February 7, 1977. According to the learned Counsel had the company raised the plea of non-resumption of Jute Division in its written statement or even at the trial the Bank would have certainly produced the relevant evidence to show that the Jute Division was created in 1972 and that its creation had no bearing or effect on the liability of the company. He, further, submitted that it is the company itself which was liable to repay the loan and not the Jute Division and its creation and transfer to the Jute Corporation or the Jute Marketing Corporation did not in any way affect the company's liability to the Bank. The liability to repay the Bank was that of the company and not of the Jute Division. 

 35. As regards the non-joinder of necessary parties and the company's contention that the suit was liable to the dismissed for such non-joinder, Dr. Hossain referred to the distinction between necessary and proper parties. 

 36. Dr. Hossain further, contended that the company could have filed an application for adding them as party under Order 1, Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The company did not make any specific allegation against the Government or against the Jute Corporation but there are only some vague allegations against the administrator in paragraph 8 of the written statement. Nor did the company pursue its claim, if any, against the Government and the Corporation concerned it the grievance against them had been so real. The learned Counsel pointed out that the High Court Division before which the appellant had raised this grievance on non-joinder of necessary parties had rightly rejected it. For the aforesaid reason and also because the claim of the Bank was against the company which is a distinct corporate entity and not against the Government and the Corporation, they were not made parties. Further, the jute stocks of the company were sold out by the administrator before September, 1972 whereas the Jute Corporation came into the picture on April 7, 1975 and the Jute Marketing Corporation on June 29, 1976. Non summoning of the administrator as to how the jute stocks were disposed of the Counsel claimed, showed that the company was not at all concerned for the absence of the Government and the Jute Corporation as a party. 

 53. Dr. Hossain pointed out that this was not a correct statement. He submitted that even if this claim is conceded, there is no explanation whatsoever as to why no representation to the Government or the Jute Marketing Corporation was made as to the jute stocks or the liability to repay the loan to the Bank in the subsequent years when the alleged threat to their lives and property no more existed. That the company or its directors did not move the Government is admitted by D.W.1 in his cross-examination. For, he said "we did not make any representation to the Jute Corporation about the jute stock. We made representations to the Government for release". In the written statement also which was filed at the end of two years after the filing of the plaint, there is no mention of the actual quantity of jute taken over by the Government except making a passing reference that "the cash credit limit and the overdraft limit used to be granted against pledge and hypothecation of jute stocks which were always sufficient to cover the advances actually made by the Bank from time to time". Nor is there any reference in the written statement regarding the liability of the Government or the Corporation for taking over the jute stocks as well as not returning them to or non-resumption of the Jute Division by the company. On the other hand, from the minutes of the meeting held in the Chamber of kazi Anwarul Haque, Adviser-in-charge of the Ministry of Jute held on September 6, 1976 it appears that Mr. M.M. Ispahani agreed on the following matters: 

 59. So far as the non-impleading of the Jute Corporation or Jute Marketing Corporation or the Government is concerned the above conclusion regarding the subsistence of the appellant company's liability to repay the loan to the Bank negatives the necessity of making any one of them party in the suit. The relationship of creditor and debtor does not admit of the introduction of any other person in a suit filed by one against the other, for determining their relationship as such creditor or debtor in respect of a loan transaction, unless such other person or persons are in any way formally connected with it, by formally according to share any obligation arising from such loan. To my mind it seems that only a guarantor or a co-mortgagor or assignee of the debtor's interest or liability may be made a party to such suit. As the company including the three subsidiary companies has already been returned, the question before us is not as to what would have been the position if the company including the three subsidiary companies were not released by the Government, but the question is whether after the release the company is still liable for its debts previous to the taking over by the Government. From the foregoing discussion it appears that the company must be held responsible for the repayment of the loan excluding what has already been paid to the Bank. 

 61. Whatever liability the Government or Jute Corporation or Jute Marketing Corporation may have incurred in respect of the loan under consideration cannot be determined in this suit. It would, therefore, be seen that none of them is a necessary party in the suit which is not liable to be dismissed on this ground. It is also not necessary to send the case back for impleading them. 

 63. What led them not to appear before the courts and put up defence, if any, such nonappearance does not certainly strengthen the position either of themselves or of the company. They are equally liable to repay the loan under consideration and so far as the priority in repaying is concerned it is for the respondent Bank to choose whether it will proceed against them first or the company in the matter of realising their outstanding dues.
